label: Optimization and Lagrange Multipliers
notes: Appendix D occupies only printed pages 597 and 598, yet it underwrites redundancy resolution, control allocation, and contact reasoning across the whole book. We frame the chapter question: what does a multiplier tell us geometrically about constrained robot decisions, and why the normal direction is the key character.

label: Unconstrained Optimality
notes: Before adding constraints we recall plain optimality. A smooth cost is stationary where its gradient vanishes, and the Hessian's sign decides minimum, maximum, or saddle. This second-order test reappears later as the curvature margin along feasible motion, so we anchor it firmly on pages 597 to 598.

label: Adding an Equality Constraint
notes: Now we restrict the design variable to a constraint surface defined by g equals zero. Feasible first-order motion must stay tangent to that surface, meaning the constraint gradient is orthogonal to any allowed step. This tangent-space restriction is the geometric heart of everything that follows in Appendix D.

label: The Lagrange Condition
notes: At a constrained optimum no feasible tangent direction lowers the cost, so the cost gradient has no tangent component left. The only place it can point is along the constraint normal. That forces grad f plus lambda grad g to vanish, the stationarity equation that names the multiplier lambda.

label: The Lagrangian
notes: We package the condition by forming the Lagrangian, cost plus lambda times constraint. Setting its gradient with respect to the design variable and the multiplier to zero recovers both stationarity and feasibility at once. This bookkeeping device scales cleanly to several constraints stacked as a vector g with a vector lambda.

label: Geometric Picture
notes: The picture to memorize: at the optimum a level curve of the cost is tangent to the constraint curve, and the two gradients are parallel. The multiplier is exactly the signed ratio that rescales the constraint normal onto the cost gradient. We draw the opposing arrows so the sign of lambda becomes visible.

label: Worked Example
notes: We minimize a weighted distance to a target that sits outside an elliptical constraint, so the optimum lives on the boundary. The notebook reports tiny constraint and stationarity residuals and a positive curvature margin near 2.83, confirming the gradients align and the feasible second derivative is genuinely a minimum.

label: Inequality Constraints and KKT
notes: Real robots face inequalities like joint limits and friction cones. The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions extend Lagrange with multiplier sign restrictions and complementary slackness, so an inactive constraint carries a zero multiplier and contributes no normal. Active-set reasoning decides which constraints actually touch the solution before any signs are checked.

label: Robotics Applications
notes: The same normal-versus-tangent split powers least-squares redundancy resolution through the pseudoinverse, minimum-effort torque selection subject to a task wrench, and contact reasoning where a surface normal supplies reaction force but no tangential work. One geometric idea quietly organizes planning, control allocation, and force distribution alike.

label: Debugging With Residuals
notes: Because the theory is geometric, it is also testable. A trustworthy candidate satisfies the constraint, drives the stationarity vector small, shows a near-zero directional derivative along the feasible tangent, and keeps a positive curvature margin. These four residuals turn Appendix D into a practical instrument for catching implementation mistakes.

label: Recap
notes: To close: a Lagrange multiplier measures how strongly a constraint normal must be invoked to balance the cost gradient. Optimality means level set tangent to constraint, gradients parallel, feasible tangent improvement zero. Carry the normal-tangent decomposition into every constrained robot decision you meet after pages 597 and 598.
